questions.why: Normal sinus features at a rate under 60 define sinus bradycardia. A junctional escape rhythm at 40 to 60 would lack normal upright preceding P waves.

questions.q: Which finding is a common physiologic cause of sinus bradycardia rather than a pathologic one?
questions.why: Well conditioned athletes commonly have resting rates below 60 because of increased stroke volume and vagal tone. Fever and hyperthyroidism both drive the rate up and would produce sinus tachycardia.

questions.q: A patient with a fever of 103 degrees Fahrenheit has a regular rhythm at 122 beats per minute with an upright P wave preceding every narrow QRS. The rhythm is:
questions.why: Identifiable sinus P waves before each QRS at 100 to 160 beats per minute define sinus tachycardia, and fever is a classic cause. Supraventricular tachycardia typically runs 150 to 250 with P waves hidden in the preceding T wave.

questions.q: A tracing shows upright P waves before every narrow QRS with a constant PR interval, but the R-R intervals shorten with inspiration and lengthen with expiration. This describes:
questions.why: Cyclic variation in R-R tied to the respiratory cycle with otherwise normal sinus features is sinus arrhythmia, a benign finding common in the young. Wandering atrial pacemaker would show at least three different P wave shapes, which are absent here.

questions.q: A strip shows regular sinus beats interrupted by a flat pause during which no P wave or QRS appears; the underlying rhythm then resumes. The pause is not a multiple of the prior R-R. This represents:
questions.why: Absence of both the P wave and the QRS indicates the sinus node failed to fire, which is sinus arrest. In Mobitz II the P wave still appears on time and only the QRS is dropped.

questions.q: Sick sinus syndrome most characteristically produces which pattern?
choices: A fixed rate of exactly 60 with no variation
Alternating episodes of bradycardia and tachycardia
Progressive PR lengthening with dropped beats
Wide QRS complexes at 20 to 40 beats per minute
questions.why: Sick sinus syndrome, also called the tachy-brady syndrome, alternates inappropriately slow and fast supraventricular rates. Progressive PR lengthening with a dropped beat is Wenckebach, an AV node problem rather than sinus node dysfunction.

questions.q: An early beat appears with a P wave of abnormal shape, a narrow QRS, and a pause afterward that is less than fully compensatory. This beat is a:
questions.why: An early abnormal P wave with a narrow QRS and a noncompensatory pause is a premature atrial complex, because the ectopic atrial impulse resets the sinus node. A premature ventricular complex would be wide and bizarre with no preceding P wave.

questions.q: A strip shows an irregular rhythm at 82 beats per minute in which the P waves display three clearly different shapes and the PR intervals vary. This rhythm is:
questions.why: At least three P wave morphologies with varying PR intervals at a rate under 100 defines wandering atrial pacemaker. The identical picture at a rate over 100 would instead be called multifocal atrial tachycardia.

questions.q: Multifocal atrial tachycardia is distinguished from wandering atrial pacemaker chiefly by:
choices: The presence of wide QRS complexes
A ventricular rate exceeding 100 beats per minute
Absence of any identifiable P waves
questions.why: Both show at least three P wave morphologies and irregular rhythm; the rate over 100 defines multifocal atrial tachycardia. P waves are present in both, so absence of P waves fits atrial fibrillation instead.

questions.q: A narrow-complex tachycardia at 190 beats per minute is perfectly regular and no P waves can be identified, though the T waves appear unusually peaked. The most likely rhythm is:
choices: Atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response
questions.why: A regular narrow-complex rhythm at 150 to 250 with P waves buried in the preceding T wave is supraventricular tachycardia. Atrial fibrillation is ruled out because the rhythm is regular rather than irregularly irregular.

questions.q: A tracing shows a sawtooth baseline with identical flutter waves at an atrial rate of about 300 per minute and a regular ventricular response of 150. The conduction ratio is:
questions.why: An atrial rate of 300 with a ventricular rate of 150 means every other flutter wave conducts, a 2 to 1 ratio. A 4 to 1 ratio at the same atrial rate would produce a ventricular rate near 75.

questions.q: The atrial rate in typical atrial flutter usually falls in which range?
questions.why: Classic atrial flutter has an atrial rate of 250 to 350 per minute, most often near 300. Rates over 400 with a chaotic baseline indicate atrial fibrillation instead.

questions.q: A tracing shows an irregularly irregular ventricular rhythm at 118 beats per minute, no discernible P waves, and a chaotic wavering baseline. This rhythm is:
choices: Atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response
questions.why: Absent P waves with a chaotic fibrillatory baseline and an irregularly irregular ventricular response is atrial fibrillation. Atrial flutter would show uniform sawtooth waves rather than a chaotic baseline.

questions.q: The major complication that makes atrial fibrillation clinically dangerous even when the rate is controlled is:
choices: Thromboembolic stroke from atrial blood stasis
Permanent loss of the AV node
questions.why: Ineffective atrial contraction allows blood to pool and form clots that can embolize to the brain, which is why anticoagulation is standard. Atrial fibrillation does not directly convert to ventricular fibrillation.

questions.q: Which P wave finding is characteristic of a junctional rhythm?
choices: Peaked P waves taller than 2.5 mm
Two P waves for every QRS
Inverted before the QRS, absent, or following the QRS
questions.why: Because the junctional impulse depolarizes the atria retrograde, the P wave is inverted, hidden, or appears after the QRS. Two P waves per QRS suggests a 2 to 1 AV block, not a junctional focus.

questions.q: When a P wave is visible ahead of the QRS in a junctional rhythm, the PR interval is typically:
questions.why: Retrograde atrial activation from the AV junction reaches the atria quickly, producing a short PR of less than 0.12 second. A PR greater than 0.20 second defines first-degree AV block and is not a junctional feature.

questions.q: A regular rhythm at 48 beats per minute shows narrow QRS complexes with inverted P waves immediately preceding each QRS and a PR interval of 0.08 second. This is:
questions.why: The intrinsic rate of the AV junction is 40 to 60, so 48 with inverted P waves and a short PR is a junctional escape rhythm. Idioventricular rhythm would have wide QRS complexes at 20 to 40.

questions.q: A regular narrow-complex rhythm at 88 beats per minute shows no visible P waves before the QRS complexes but small retrograde P waves after them. This is best identified as:
questions.why: A junctional focus firing at 60 to 100 is termed accelerated junctional rhythm. Normal sinus rhythm requires upright P waves before each QRS, which are absent here.

questions.q: A premature junctional complex is identified by an early beat with:
choices: A wide bizarre QRS and full compensatory pause
An early upright P wave with a PR of 0.18 second
A narrow QRS with an inverted or absent P wave
A pause exactly twice the underlying R-R
questions.why: A premature junctional complex arises above the ventricles, so the QRS stays narrow while the P wave is inverted, absent, or retrograde. A wide bizarre QRS with a compensatory pause describes a premature ventricular complex.

questions.q: A beat occurs early, has no preceding P wave, measures 0.16 second in width, appears bizarre, and is followed by a full compensatory pause. This beat is a:
questions.why: Width over 0.12 second with no preceding P wave and a full compensatory pause is the classic premature ventricular complex. A premature atrial complex would be narrow with an early abnormal P wave.

questions.q: On a strip, all premature ventricular complexes look identical to one another. These are described as:
questions.why: Identical morphology indicates all ectopic beats arise from a single ventricular focus, which is unifocal. Multifocal complexes vary in shape because they originate from different sites and carry greater concern.

questions.q: A rhythm strip shows one sinus beat followed by one premature ventricular complex, repeating throughout the strip. This pattern is called:
questions.why: Bigeminy means every other beat is a premature ventricular complex. Trigeminy would show one ectopic beat after every two normal beats.

questions.q: Two premature ventricular complexes occurring back to back with no intervening sinus beat are termed a:
questions.why: Two consecutive premature ventricular complexes form a couplet; three or more in a row is a run of ventricular tachycardia. Quadrigeminy describes an ectopic beat after every three normal beats, not paired beats.

questions.q: The R-on-T phenomenon is dangerous because a premature ventricular complex landing on the T wave may:
choices: Trigger ventricular tachycardia or ventricular fibrillation
questions.why: The T wave marks the vulnerable relative refractory period, and a stimulus there can provoke lethal ventricular arrhythmias. Resetting the sinus node is a property of atrial ectopy and is not the danger being described.

questions.q: A tracing shows wide bizarre QRS complexes at a regular rate of 32 beats per minute with no P waves. This rhythm is:
questions.why: A ventricular escape pacemaker at 20 to 40 with wide complexes and absent P waves is an idioventricular rhythm. Accelerated idioventricular rhythm looks identical but runs at 40 to 100.

questions.q: Wide QRS complexes with no P waves at a regular rate of 65 beats per minute, often seen after reperfusion therapy, best fits:
questions.why: A ventricular focus firing between 40 and 100 defines accelerated idioventricular rhythm, a common reperfusion rhythm. Ventricular tachycardia by definition exceeds 100 beats per minute.

questions.q: A regular wide-complex rhythm at 170 beats per minute shows QRS complexes all of the same shape with no identifiable P waves. This is:
questions.why: Uniform wide complexes over 100 beats per minute without P waves is monomorphic ventricular tachycardia. Supraventricular tachycardia would show narrow QRS complexes unless aberrancy is present.

questions.q: A wide-complex tachycardia shows QRS complexes whose amplitude and polarity progressively twist around the baseline in a spindle pattern. This rhythm is:
questions.why: The twisting axis around the isoelectric line is the hallmark of torsades de pointes, a polymorphic ventricular tachycardia. Ventricular fibrillation has no organized QRS complexes at all, whereas torsades still shows recognizable complexes.

questions.q: Torsades de pointes is most strongly associated with which underlying abnormality?
choices: A prolonged QT interval, often with low magnesium
A shortened QT interval from hypercalcemia
questions.why: Torsades arises in the setting of QT prolongation, frequently with hypomagnesemia or hypokalemia, and magnesium is the usual treatment. A short QT from hypercalcemia is the opposite electrophysiologic setting.

questions.q: A monitor shows chaotic, completely disorganized undulations with no identifiable P waves, QRS complexes, or T waves, and the patient is unresponsive without a pulse. This rhythm is:
questions.why: Totally disorganized waveforms with no recognizable complexes in a pulseless patient is ventricular fibrillation, which requires immediate defibrillation. Pulseless electrical activity would show organized complexes on the monitor despite the absent pulse.

questions.q: Fine ventricular fibrillation differs from coarse ventricular fibrillation mainly in that fine ventricular fibrillation:
choices: Has lower amplitude waveforms and usually indicates a longer downtime
questions.why: Fine ventricular fibrillation has smaller amplitude undulations and generally reflects a longer arrest interval with a poorer prognosis. Neither form produces identifiable QRS complexes or a pulse.

questions.q: Before calling asystole, the technician should:
choices: Increase the paper speed to 50 mm per second
Switch the machine to diagnostic filter mode
Confirm the flat line in at least two different leads and check lead connections
Print a full 12-lead before touching the patient
questions.why: A flat line can result from a disconnected lead or fine ventricular fibrillation viewed in one vector, so asystole must be confirmed in two leads with connections checked. Changing paper speed does nothing to distinguish true asystole from artifact.

questions.q: A patient has no palpable pulse, yet the monitor shows an organized rhythm with narrow QRS complexes at 70 beats per minute. This situation is called:
questions.why: Organized electrical activity without a mechanical pulse defines pulseless electrical activity. Asystole would show a flat line rather than organized complexes.

questions.q: An agonal rhythm is best described as:
choices: Very slow, wide, irregular complexes that gradually diminish, seen in dying patients
A regular narrow rhythm at 55 beats per minute
A sawtooth pattern at 300 atrial beats per minute
Alternating tall and short QRS complexes at a normal rate
questions.why: Agonal rhythm shows sparse, wide, dying ventricular complexes progressing toward asystole. A sawtooth pattern describes atrial flutter, a perfusing supraventricular rhythm with an entirely different meaning.

questions.q: A tracing shows an upright P wave before every QRS, a regular rate of 68, narrow QRS complexes, and a constant PR interval of 0.26 second. This is:
choices: Normal sinus rhythm with a wandering baseline
questions.why: A constant PR interval greater than 0.20 second with every P wave conducted is first-degree AV block. Mobitz I would show the PR lengthening progressively until a QRS is dropped.

questions.q: A strip shows the PR interval lengthening on each successive beat until a P wave appears with no QRS following it, then the cycle repeats. This is:
questions.why: Progressive PR prolongation ending in a dropped QRS is Mobitz I, also called Wenckebach. In Mobitz II the PR interval stays constant before the beat is dropped.

questions.q: A strip shows a constant PR interval of 0.18 second with narrow QRS complexes, but every third P wave is suddenly not followed by a QRS. This is:
questions.why: A constant PR with sudden unexpected dropped QRS complexes is Mobitz II, which reflects block below the AV node and often progresses to complete block. Mobitz I is excluded because the PR does not lengthen before the drop.

questions.q: A tracing shows two P waves for every QRS complex with a constant PR interval on the conducted beats. This pattern is described as:
questions.why: A fixed 2 to 1 ratio of P waves to QRS complexes with consistent PR intervals is 2 to 1 AV block, which cannot be classified as Mobitz I or II from the ratio alone. Complete heart block is excluded because there is a consistent relationship between the P waves and the QRS complexes.

questions.q: A strip shows P waves marching out regularly at 88 per minute and wide QRS complexes marching out regularly at 34 per minute, with no consistent relationship between them. This is:
choices: Sinus bradycardia with premature ventricular complexes
questions.why: Independent atrial and ventricular rates with complete AV dissociation define third-degree block, here with a ventricular escape pacemaker. Mobitz II retains a fixed PR on conducted beats, which is absent when dissociation is complete.

questions.q: Which pair of AV blocks is considered the most dangerous and most likely to require pacing?
questions.why: Mobitz II and complete heart block involve infranodal disease, carry unreliable escape rhythms, and often require a pacemaker. First-degree block and Wenckebach are usually benign and are frequently observed without intervention.

questions.q: A bundle branch block is first suspected on the ECG when the QRS duration is:
choices: Exactly equal to the PR interval
questions.why: Delayed activation of one ventricle widens the QRS to 0.12 second or more, the threshold for bundle branch block. A QRS of 0.08 to 0.10 second is normal and excludes the diagnosis.

questions.q: An RSR prime pattern producing rabbit ears in lead V1 with a QRS of 0.14 second suggests:
questions.why: The RSR prime in V1 with a wide QRS is the signature of right bundle branch block. Left bundle branch block instead produces a broad notched R wave in V5 and V6 with a deep S in V1.

questions.q: A broad, notched, monophasic R wave in leads V5 and V6 with a QRS of 0.13 second indicates:
questions.why: Left bundle branch block delays left ventricular activation, producing broad notched R waves in the lateral leads V5 and V6. Right bundle branch block would instead show the RSR prime pattern in V1.

questions.q: A hemiblock refers to a conduction block in:
choices: One fascicle of the left bundle branch
questions.why: The left bundle divides into anterior and posterior fascicles, and block of one of them is a hemiblock, recognized largely by an axis shift. The AV node does not divide into halves, so that choice is anatomically incorrect.

questions.q: A tracing shows a sharp narrow vertical spike immediately preceding each wide QRS complex, with no spike before the P waves. This indicates:
questions.why: A single spike before a wide QRS with no atrial spike indicates ventricular pacing. A dual-chamber device would produce two spikes, one before the P wave and one before the QRS.

questions.q: A paced tracing shows pacemaker spikes that are not followed by any P wave or QRS complex. This malfunction is:
questions.why: Failure to capture means the delivered stimulus does not depolarize the myocardium, so a spike appears with no resulting complex. Failure to sense would instead show spikes appearing inappropriately after the patient's own intrinsic beats.

questions.q: A pacemaker delivers spikes at inappropriate times, including shortly after the patient's own intrinsic QRS complexes. This malfunction is:
questions.why: Failure to sense, or undersensing, means the device does not recognize intrinsic beats and paces on top of them, risking R-on-T. Oversensing is the opposite problem, where the device sees noise as a beat and withholds needed pacing.

questions.q: A pacemaker interprets muscle activity as cardiac beats and therefore withholds pacing, producing pauses. This malfunction is called:
questions.why: Oversensing causes the generator to inhibit output because it misreads noncardiac signals as intrinsic activity. Undersensing produces the opposite finding, with extra spikes rather than missing ones.

questions.q: Horizontal or downsloping ST segment depression of 1 mm or more measured at the J point most suggests:
questions.why: ST depression of at least 1 mm reflects inadequate perfusion, that is, ischemia. Acute injury is indicated by ST elevation, not depression.

questions.q: Which finding meets the criterion for acute myocardial injury in the precordial leads?
choices: ST elevation of 0.5 mm in V2 alone
ST elevation of 2 mm or more in two contiguous precordial leads
T wave inversion in V1 only
ST depression of 3 mm in V4
questions.why: Precordial criteria require at least 2 mm of ST elevation in two contiguous leads, while limb leads require 1 mm in two contiguous leads. An isolated 0.5 mm elevation in one lead does not meet any injury threshold.

questions.q: A patient shows ST elevation in leads II, III, and aVF with reciprocal ST depression in I and aVL. The infarct location and usual culprit artery are:
choices: Anterior wall, left anterior descending artery
questions.why: Leads II, III, and aVF view the inferior wall, which is supplied by the right coronary artery in most people, and reciprocal depression appears in the opposite lateral leads. The left anterior descending artery supplies the anterior and septal walls seen in V1 through V4, not the inferior leads.
